reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by Borrelia recurrentis and transmitted by the human body louse; infection follows crushing of the louse so that its coelomic fluid contaminates broken skin or mucosae rather than the bite itself
Epidemic in conditions of overcrowding, poverty, cold and poor hygiene, and re-emerging among refugees and migrants travelling from endemic regions of the Horn of Africa
After an incubation of about a week there is sudden high fever, rigors, severe headache, myalgia and prostration lasting several days, followed by a crisis and an afebrile interval before relapse
Compared with the tick-borne form it typically causes fewer relapses, often only one or two, but tends to be more severe with a higher untreated mortality
Jaundice, a bleeding tendency with petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly and neurological involvement are prominent features of severe disease
Diagnosis is made by demonstrating abundant spirochaetes on a Giemsa- or Wright-stained peripheral blood film taken during fever
A single dose of an appropriate antibiotic can be curative, but the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after treatment is frequent and can be life-threatening, so patients must be closely monitored
reference.pathophysiology: Borrelia recurrentis is a spirochaete confined to humans and spread by the body louse. Once inoculated it proliferates to produce intense spirochaetaemia driving the febrile episode. Host antibody responses clear the dominant antigenic variant, but antigenic variation allows escape variants to expand and cause relapse, though fewer cycles occur than in the tick-borne disease. Heavy spirochaetal loads and the associated inflammatory response cause hepatic dysfunction with jaundice, thrombocytopenia and bleeding, splenic enlargement and neurological involvement. Antibiotic-induced mass lysis of spirochaetes releases inflammatory mediators, producing the often severe Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with abrupt rigors, hyperpyrexia and haemodynamic instability.
additionalDifferentials: Viral haemorrhagic fever in relevant epidemiological settings
additionalInvestigations: Thick and thin peripheral blood films during fever showing numerous spirochaetes
PCR of blood for Borrelia recurrentis where available
Full blood count for thrombocytopenia and anaemia
Coagulation studies given the bleeding tendency
Examination of clothing for body lice to support the diagnosis
redFlags: Severe Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with hyperpyrexia, rigors and hypotension after the first dose
Jaundice with a marked bleeding tendency
Occurrence in a crowded refugee or migrant population indicating epidemic potential
reference.prognosis: Louse-borne relapsing fever is more severe than the tick-borne form and untreated epidemics carry high mortality, but prompt antibiotic treatment is very effective; the main early hazard of treatment is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, which itself can be fatal without supportive care.
pitfalls: Underestimating the severity and life-threatening potential of the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
Not examining blood films during fever, missing the abundant spirochaetes
Failing to recognise the diagnosis in migrants from endemic regions
Neglecting delousing and public-health control measures
Confusing it with malaria and delaying appropriate antibiotics and monitoring
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat with an appropriate antibiotic such as a tetracycline (doxycycline) or a macrolide such as erythromycin, with penicillin as an alternative, to clear the spirochaetaemia
Anticipate and manage the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after the first dose with close monitoring, fluid resuscitation and supportive care, as it can be life-threatening
Provide supportive care for hepatic dysfunction, thrombocytopenia and bleeding, with fluids and blood-product support as required
Decontaminate the patient by delousing, treating clothing and improving hygiene to eliminate the body-louse vector and prevent reinfection
Screen and treat close contacts and notify public health authorities given the epidemic potential in overcrowded settings
Monitor for relapse during the afebrile interval and escalate for haemodynamic instability, severe bleeding or neurological deterioration
